module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1071

*References:*
* [erdosproblems.com/1071](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1071)
* [Da85] Danzer, L., _Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry_.
  Intuitive geometry (Siófok, 1985), 167-177.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Set Metric EuclideanGeometry Order

namespace Erdos1071

/-- Two segments are disjoint if they only intersect at their endpoints (if at all). -/
def SegmentsDisjoint (seg1 seg2 : ℝ² × ℝ²) : Prop :=
  segment ℝ seg1.1 seg1.2 ∩ segment ℝ seg2.1 seg2.2 ⊆ {seg1.1, seg1.2, seg2.1, seg2.2}

/--
Can a finite set of disjoint unit segments in a unit square be maximal?
Solved affirmatively by [Da85], who gave an explicit construction.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos1071.lean"]
theorem erdos_1071.parts.i :
    answer(True) ↔ ∃ S : Finset (ℝ² × ℝ²),
      Maximal (fun T : Finset (ℝ² × ℝ²) =>
        (∀ seg ∈ T, dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧
          seg.1 0 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧ seg.1 1 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧
          seg.2 0 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧ seg.2 1 ∈ Icc 0 1) ∧
          (T : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²)).Pairwise SegmentsDisjoint) S := by
  sorry

/-- Is there a region $R$ with a maximal set of disjoint unit line segments that is countably infinite?
Here a unit line segment is a rotated and translated copy of the open interval $(0,1)$, and it is
required to be contained in $R$.
Solved affirmatively by [Fo99], who gave an explicit construction.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos1071b.lean"]
theorem erdos_1071.parts.ii :
    answer(True) ↔ ∃ (R : Set ℝ²) (S : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²)),
      IsOpen R ∧ IsConnected R ∧ S.Countable ∧ S.Infinite ∧
      Maximal (fun T : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²) =>
        (∀ seg ∈ T, dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧ openSegment ℝ seg.1 seg.2 ⊆ R) ∧
        T.Pairwise SegmentsDisjoint) S := by
  sorry

end Erdos1071

findings.description: The module docstring's reference list gives "[Da85] Danzer, L., _Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry_. Intuitive geometry (Siófok, 1985), 167-177". `erdos_1071.parts.i`'s docstring then says "Solved affirmatively by [Da85]". That paper is by P. Erdős alone, published 1987; it is the source's [Er87b]. Danzer's example is only reported inside it (Fig. 3). No Danzer publication with this title exists, so the author and the citation key are both wrong. The mathematics is not affected.

reformulations.difference: Segments are ordered endpoint pairs. "Disjoint" means the closed segments `segment ℝ a b` and `segment ℝ c d` meet only in points of {a,b,c,d}. So shared endpoints and T-junctions (an endpoint of one lying inside the other) are allowed. The source instead speaks of disjoint rotated/translated copies of the open interval (0,1). A reader might mistake this for the [0,1] variant ("intersect only at their endpoints") or for a relaxation of "no two intersect".
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Take non-degenerate segments (a≠b, c≠d; guaranteed by `dist = 1`). (⇒) A point p in both open segments lies in both closed segments, and is none of a,b,c,d, because a point of a non-degenerate open segment is not one of its endpoints. So `SegmentsDisjoint` fails. (⇐) A point of [a,b]∩[c,d] outside {a,b,c,d} lies in both open segments, because [x,y] = {x,y} ∪ (x,y) (`insert_endpoints_openSegment`). Also, `SegmentsDisjoint` is symmetric, and (a,b),(b,a) are never `SegmentsDisjoint`. So a pairwise-disjoint family holds each geometric segment at most once, and its reversal can never be added. Hence maximality over families of pairs equals maximality over families of open unit segments. This matches the source's reading, which Bloom confirms on the forum: the original intervals are open, so endpoints may touch other segments.

reformulations.difference: "In the unit square" is encoded as all four endpoint coordinates lying in Icc 0 1, i.e. the closed square. Maximality is taken only among `Finset`s. The source's "maximal with respect to this property" ranges over all families, and "unit square" could also be read as the open square.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (1) Both endpoints lie in [0,1]² iff the open segment lies in the closed square. The closure of `openSegment` is `segment`, and the square is closed and convex (proved). (2) The admissibility predicate is hereditary. So `Maximal` among Finsets holds iff no admissible segment outside S is disjoint from every member of S, which is maximality among all families (proved: `maximal_finset_iff`). (3) Closed vs open square: a unit segment in [0,1]² with an interior point on the boundary lies on that side's line, so it is that side (each side has length exactly 1). Every other unit segment has its open part in (0,1)². The four sides are disjoint from everything else. So finite maximal families for the closed square are exactly the four sides plus a finite maximal family for the open square (argued, not formalized). I also proved in Lean that plby's `Erdos1071b.erdos_1071b` statement, restated verbatim with segments as sets `openSegment ℝ x y`, implies this right-hand side.

reformulations.difference: The source's "region" is encoded as `IsOpen R ∧ IsConnected R`, with no boundedness or convexity. "Denumerable" is encoded as `S.Countable ∧ S.Infinite`, and "in R" as `openSegment ℝ seg.1 seg.2 ⊆ R`. Closed regions such as [0,1]² are excluded as values of R.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: "Region" is undefined in the source; open connected set is its standard meaning, and Erdős says "Let R be any region". For an existence question, excluding closed regions only strengthens the claim. The source's recorded witness is the unit square, which is available in open form: plby `Erdos1071.Corollary_2` gives a countably infinite maximal family in (0,1)². I proved in Lean that this statement, restated verbatim, implies the right-hand side with R = the open unit square. That R is open and connected (convex and nonempty). The pair-encoded family is countably infinite because endpoint choice is injective, and it is maximal. So the answer `True` holds under either reading.

review.notes:
Summary: both theorems state the source's two questions faithfully, with the correct answer (True) and category (solved). The defects are reference slips in the docstrings and swapped formal_proof links.

Primary text (Er87b pp. 173–174, OCR checked twice):
- Question 1: "Can one find a finite set of unit intervals in the unit square, no two of which intersect and which are maximal with respect to this property? ... Danzer found a simple example (Fig.3)".
- Variant: "... if we insist that the only common point two of our intervals can have is their endpoint".
- Question 2: "Let R be any region and let there be given in R a maximal set of disjoint unit intervals. Can such a set ever be denumerable?"

Lean checks in /workspace/review:
- equiv1.lean: `SegmentsDisjoint` is symmetric; for non-degenerate segments it is equivalent to disjointness of the open segments; a segment and its reversal are never `SegmentsDisjoint`.
- equiv2.lean: the endpoint condition holds iff the open segment lies in the closed square.
- equiv3.lean: `Maximal` over Finsets is equivalent to the blocking condition.
- transfer.lean: plby's statements (sets of open segments), restated verbatim, imply both FC right-hand sides. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.
- I could not compile plby's own proofs here (they target Lean v4.24.0), but both files are sorry-free and axiom-free.

For maintainers, not reported as findings:
1. `parts.ii` follows Erdős's literal "any region". As Alexeev notes on the source's forum, that literal question has a cheap witness: thin ellipses with major axis 1, joined by thin tunnels, whose only unit segments are the major axes. So the formal statement is much weaker than the unit-square result the source records. A variant fixing R to the unit square would capture what was actually proved.
2. The `SegmentsDisjoint` docstring ("only intersect at their endpoints") is loosely worded. The definition correctly allows T-junctions, and it is not the [0,1] variant.
3. The [0,1] variant (closed intervals meeting only at common endpoints) is not formalized.
4. Both formal_proof links point at `blob/main` instead of a pinned commit.
